C20 The Canon · Reading Layer

History & Judgment

Lesson Lectures · learn

Every framework you've learned so far hands you a clean answer. History hands you judgment instead — the slower, harder skill of reading a situation correctly before you reach for a tool. The strategist's edge is rarely a better calculation; it's seeing which game you're really in, noticing when an advantage has quietly turned into overreach, and catching the historical analogy you're applying without testing it. This lesson assembles that judgment from four of the oldest and most-used books on the shelf: a Greek general writing in 400 BCE, a Prussian officer after Napoleon, and a Harvard scholar dissecting the thirteen days that nearly ended the world. Tap the cards, the diagrams, and the quizzes as you go.

1 · The oldest pattern: rising power, ruling power, and fear

The first case study in strategy was written by Thucydides, an Athenian general, about the war that destroyed his own city's empire. His diagnosis of why it happened is still the most-quoted sentence in the field: war became likely not from any single villain, but from a structural shift — a rising power frightening an established one. Harvard's Graham Allison gave the pattern a name in 2017.

"A ruling power being challenged for hegemony from a newer rising power has happened many different times throughout recorded history. In 2017 Harvard Professor Graham Allison recognized this and coined the term Thucydides Trap to describe such events."

— Lesser Known History, "Thucydides Trap: From Sparta and Athens to Its Modern Context" · in your corpus

The crucial move — and the reason this is a judgment lesson, not a doom prophecy — is what Allison says about the word "inevitable." The original Greek does not mean certain. Tap each bar to see how his 500-year tally actually breaks down.

"I look at the last 500 years and find 16 cases in which this happened; 12 of them end in war… If you look at the number of places Thucydides uses terms like the one that gets translated 'inevitable' — he doesn't mean inevitable the way we might think it means 100 percent. He means very, very, very likely; it's baked into the structure of the situation, but not a hundred percent."

— Graham Allison, Munich Security Conference 2020 · in your corpus

2 · Overreach: how the strong destroy themselves

Thucydides' deepest lesson isn't about rivals at all — it's that dominant powers usually lose to their own ambition. Athens didn't fall because Sparta out-fought it; it fell after the Sicilian Expedition, a wildly over-ambitious campaign launched past the point where its strength could sustain it. Clausewitz, writing 2,200 years later, gave this its precise name: the culminating point — the moment in any advance where effort outruns strength and pushing further becomes self-destruction.

The danger is that overreach often hides behind an apparently safe situation. Allison's favorite reality-check is 1914: Britain and Germany were so economically intertwined that the best-selling book in Europe argued war had become impossible. The markets agreed.

"The most famous book in Europe was written by a man named Norman Angell, called The Great Illusion — the illusion that nations could fight wars anymore, because the victor will lose more than he could gain… So neither Britain nor Germany would ever have a war. But they did."

— Graham Allison, Berggruen Institute, "The Thucydides Trap" · in your corpus

The trigger wasn't a grand decision but a small, manageable-looking event that the rigid system couldn't absorb — an assassination that "didn't even make the front page in London or New York," yet "within five weeks had dragged all the great nations of Europe into a war." Interdependence felt like a safeguard; it wasn't. The judgment skill is to ask where your own culminating point is before you sail for Sicily.

3 · Friction: why the plan is never the reality

If Thucydides teaches you to read the strategic landscape, Clausewitz teaches you to distrust your own plan once you start moving. His master-concept is friction: the gap between the textbook and the world. Everything in war, he wrote, is simple — but the simplest thing is difficult.

"It's like that saying, 'no plan survives contact with the enemy.' It's easy to sit there with the map out and be like, 'all right, we're going to do this' — but then [reality]… he's like, hold on, there's real friction."

— DoctrineLM, "Clausewitz On War, Book 1 Ch.7: Friction in War | NotebookLM Podcast" · in your corpus

The companion idea is the fog of war — and the corpus is emphatic that this is a business condition, not just a battlefield one. The fog is partly informational and partly human: people are not machines.

"You're in a negotiation closing a deal, or you're a manager — you have three major initiatives happening, teams all over the state… what's the competitor thinking, what's the customer thinking? All these elements of uncertainty — what we call the fog of war."

— The Chaos School, "EDGE Challenges – Clausewitz #6: Friction in War and the Fog of War" · in your corpus

The practical takeaway from a society that re-runs 19th-century war games is brutal and familiar to any operator: you assume you'll have "real-time intelligence and radio communications and subordinates that actually know how to follow orders… and then all of that gets messed up." Real-time clarity is a fantasy. Strategy under Clausewitz means acting decisively despite the fog, holding to your purpose while expecting the method to break.

4 · The same decision, three different stories

Now the most useful single tool in the cluster. When an organization does something that looks irrational, you almost certainly explained it with the wrong model. Graham Allison's Essence of Decision dissects the Cuban Missile Crisis through three lenses — and shows the same event tells three different stories.

Why did the U.S. choose a naval blockade over an airstrike on the missile sites? The clean "rational actor" story says blockade was the optimal choice. The corpus says otherwise:

"The air strike was not chosen because time was too short. The air force had no protocol for training and operationalizing an air strike in the amount of time they had at their disposal. Since the navy could respond more quickly, the naval blockade option became more viable."

— All About Defense, "Graham Allison's 3 Models of Foreign Policy" · in your corpus

That is Model II in one move: the decision was an output of which organization already had a runnable routine, not of optimized interest. Tap each lens to see how each one reframes the same crisis.

"A resultant under Model III does not always presuppose intention — it is simply how all of these players' activities add up to create a whole, sometimes not a very integrated or well-organized whole."

— Candy Young, "Introduction to Essence of Decision's 3 Models" · in your corpus

Exactly the right worry — and it's the framework's famous weakness. With three lenses you can explain anything after the fact, so the models are far stronger as understanding than as prediction; Model III in particular "explains everything and therefore predicts little." It can even become a sophisticated excuse — "it's just politics" — that lets bad decisions off the hook. Use it not to forecast, but to stop yourself defaulting to Model I. As Allison quotes JFK: "the essence of ultimate decision remains impenetrable to the observer, often indeed to the decider himself." Humility is the point.

5 · The reflex to discipline: history by analogy

Here is the trap every decision-maker falls into, usually without noticing. Faced with something new, the mind instantly reaches for a past parallel — "this is another Munich," "this is another Vietnam" — and then applies it wholesale. Neustadt & May's Thinking in Time is the discipline for using analogies without being used by them: before the parallel drives the decision, force a two-column list of likenesses and differences, and ruthlessly separate what you know from what you merely presume.

Allison models the discipline on his own analogy. The 1914 comparison resembles US–China today — deeply interdependent economies — so interdependence feels like a peace guarantee. The differences test says: in 1914 they were just as intertwined, and they fought anyway. Resemblance is not structural similarity. He also names the bias that makes the analogy hard to handle honestly:

"Unless Americans could imagine being comfortably adjusting to maybe even being number two in some respects… which is pretty hard to imagine for red, white and blue Americans like you and me — it certainly doesn't feel right for me. I think the US should be number one in everything; it's almost a matter of religion."

— Graham Allison, Munich Security Conference 2020 · in your corpus

That candor is the method working: name the emotion driving the analogy, separate the known from the presumed, list the differences — then decide.

6 · The vocabulary — flip to learn

The exact terms the canon uses. Tap a card to flip it.

7 · Putting it together: a judgment checklist

These four books aren't competing theories — they're a sequence of questions to run on any high-stakes call. Tap each stage.

Worked example — a market-leader's "obvious" expansion. You run the dominant player in your category and the board wants a bold push into an adjacent market. Run the checklist. Thucydides: is this your Sicilian Expedition — ambition past your culminating point, dressed up as momentum? The booming numbers are no all-clear; markets priced 1914 as peace. Clausewitz: assume the launch plan breaks on contact — distribution, hiring, a competitor's response you can't see through the fog — and keep the strategic purpose (not the launch date) supreme. Allison: when your own org keeps choosing the slower option, don't assume it's irrational — it's probably the team with the runnable playbook (Model II) or a turf win for one VP (Model III). Neustadt & May: someone will say "this is just like when we entered Region X and crushed it." Force the differences list first — and you may find the only real likeness is that you want it to be the same.

8 · Check yourself

Allison found 16 historical cases of a rising power challenging a ruling one. What does the count actually show?

12 of 16 ended in war, but 4 did not. Allison stresses the Greek "inevitable" means very likely, baked into the structure — not 100%. The four escapes are the whole point: the trap can be steered out of.

The U.S. chose a naval blockade over an airstrike in the Cuban Missile Crisis. Through Allison's lens, the deepest reason was:

This is Model II — Organizational Process. The decision was an output of which organization already had a deployable routine, not of pure optimized interest. The clean "rational actor" story explains the least.

A colleague says: "This expansion is just like when we entered Region X and won." The Neustadt & May move is to:

Force the two-column list. The error is applying a parallel wholesale; surface resemblance isn't structural similarity. Separate what you know from what you merely presume — most errors come from treating presumptions as facts.

⚠️ These are lenses for judgment, not laws for prediction

The seductive error is to treat any of these as a deterministic engine. The Thucydides Trap is probabilistic — call it a law and you've made exactly the wholesale-analogy mistake Neustadt & May warn against. Allison's three models can explain anything after the fact, so they're far better at understanding than forecasting — and "it's just politics" can become an excuse that lets bad calls off the hook. And the war metaphor itself misleads in business: most commerce is positive-sum and repeated, not a zero-sum fight to destroy an enemy, so "crush the competitor" thinking misses complementors, customers, and the larger game. Use the concepts — friction, the culminating point, the three lenses, likenesses-and-differences — never the militarism, and never as a crystal ball.

🔎 One subtlety → your bridge to the rest of the shelf

Notice the throughline running under all four books: the gap between how a decision looks and how it actually got made. Clausewitz's friction is that gap between plan and reality; Allison's models are that gap between "rational choice" and "organizational output"; Neustadt & May's discipline closes the gap between the analogy you feel and the one that fits. That single move — distrusting the clean story and asking how the sausage was really made — is the hidden engine under decision science (we're predictably irrational), organizational behavior (where you stand depends on where you sit), and systems thinking (structure drives behavior). The deepest judgment isn't knowing more history; it's catching yourself reaching for the tidy explanation, and pausing long enough to check which game you're actually in.

🎯 Your move

Pick one live, high-stakes call you're facing (a launch, a hire, a market entry, a confrontation). On paper, run the four-question checklist: (1) Thucydides — where is your culminating point, the ambition that could overextend you, and what calm are you mistaking for safety? (2) Clausewitz — name one way the plan will break on contact, and write the purpose that must survive even if the method doesn't. (3) Allison — take one "why did they decide that?" inside your org and re-explain it three ways (rational interest / standard routine / internal politics); usually it's not #1. (4) Neustadt & May — catch one "this is just like ___" and write two columns, likenesses and differences. Which column is longer? That answer is your judgment.

In the 1960s, we had the height of realism. We have a reflection on the rationality of the State, the predominance of power, and strategic choices based on the rationality of the State. Strategic stability demands that you trust the rationality of the actor you are interacting with. In this, an actor doesn't attack because he doesn't see the benefit of attacking. The opponent is supposed to think the same way. However, in reality, we have the possibility that they could think differently. The problem is that, especially after the Missile Crisis, due to the fact that we had reached such a point of tension, it generated confidence in this risky idea.

Once there is a difference of opinion, this makes the scenario more complex. The 1970s, along with a whole set of criticisms that realist thinking suffered, there was also a critique of strategic thinking based on these realistic premises, which seek to focus on the decision-making process. By understanding the decision-making process, we can understand its complexity and the type of bargain we are proposing to place the world in that direction. In this, one of the seminal works in this discussion is the work of author Graham Allison in the book “The Essence of Decision'', in which he will try to use information about American and Soviet decision-making to analyze, through different analytical models, how the set of events materialized in that way, and the extent to which realists are right to be so confident that strategic rationality would necessarily lead to this kind of result, that we observe at the end of the missile crisis.

So, he divided the analysis of that scenario into three models. The first model is the rational actor model. The rational actor model is the one the realist would use. For the realist, observing the crisis in Cuba, he realizes that from the point of view of Soviet decision-making, it makes sense to send missiles to Cuba because, in view of Cuba's change in regime, the country offers the Soviet Union a strategic opportunity that Soviets could not lose. So, it is rational, from the point of view of power distribution and from the point of view of decisively modifying the distribution of power, that the Soviets were willing to place their missiles on Cuban territory.

From an American decision-making point of view, it would be rational to create a naval blockade. That's because doing nothing and letting the missiles arrive would give a show of weakness that would invite the Soviets to actually use these missiles. Attacking the Soviet convoy as it is heading towards Cuba would be an early declaration of war, which could effectively trigger the nuclear war you don't want to trigger. So, the most rational decision is the naval blockade. Since the problem with deterrence is that, in this scenario, no one has the capacity to take the initiative, the Soviets also need to be rational and not force a war.

In this, as a result of what we call strategic stability, neither side wants war. The Soviets get what they want, they strategically position an ally to their advantage, shift the distribution of power and stage a show of force. And Americans get what they want, since despite that, they maintain the scenario of stability in which no one is willing to start a war with unpredictable consequences and the cost of which they are unwilling to pay. So, this is the realist reading of that scenario, in which, from a rational point of view and from a distribution of capabilities, this is what should be done.

They avoid putting themselves in the position where they have no choice but to trigger nuclear conflict. We also have another model, it's an organizational policy model. It is the dynamics of organizations and the working protocols of organizations. Even as a decision maker, between you ordering something done and carrying out that process, we have a lot of steps, which we don't have direct control over most of them. Processes, protocols, tools that are already installed in a certain place, which are decisive in the process of implementing a decision, are very important for us to understand exactly why a certain scenario happened and others did not.

For example, in the Cuban Crisis, the Soviets had a missile distribution apparatus, which placed these missiles in strategic spaces in Eastern Europe. But having a protocol and equipment, a transport logistics for installing this material within Eastern Europe is one thing. When we had to install the materials in Cuba, the American satellite was able to notice ships embarking in Cuba. But on these boats, they start to unload material and install factories with tents with communist symbols that can be seen from afar. In Cuba, it made them more easily discovered. Once we have the crisis in place, the Americans need to decide how they are going to react to the blockade.

Contrary to what appears within the American narrative that the naval blockade was the most reasonable alternative, the American decision-making process did not know which was the most reasonable alternative. At that point, we even had some who defended the air attack. Allison argues why airstrikes were not chosen. It wasn't because it wasn't more rational or more realistic. The air strike was not chosen because time was too short. The air force had no protocol for training and operationalizing an air strike in the amount of time they had at their disposal. Since the navy could respond more quickly, the naval blockade option became a more viable option than the air strike option.

In other circumstances there could be a very different result. In addition, we have another model: the government policy model. We saw the realist model, which doesn't look too much into the state, and infers all rationality based on the calculation of the distribution of power. The author pointed out the organizational policy model that observes bureaucracy, what happens between the moment the decision is made and the moment it is executed by the bureaucracy. But the author says that we should also look at political leaders who are actually operating, as they play multiple political games simultaneously.

Therefore, we have elements to be taken into account when making a decision like this, which are not necessarily linked to the distribution of power in the international system. It is related to the very stability of that political leadership, in the political position he or she occupies at that moment. If we look at both Kennedy and Khrushchev, we have two very particular political leaders. Why does Krushev place missiles in Cuba? Among other things, it was because within the Soviet communist party, the failure to manage the issue of the air blockade of Berlin, which was in the year before the year of the Missile Crisis, left it in a politically fragile position.

He was afraid of being knocked down and he thought he needed a show of strength. Cuba offered him an international opportunity to rebalance the game with the Americans, and an opportunity to demonstrate strength and stabilize his power within the Soviet bureaucracy. Kennedy had just come out of a failed military intervention, the attempt to invade Cuba with the Bay of Pigs invasion. So Kennedy is weakened in a context where we have elections in the US, where the Democrats were weakened. So this whole set of domestic elements creates a political circumstance that makes Kennedy not willing to take an absolute risk from the standpoint of his personality, but neither could he show weakness at the time.

Given how that conflict ends, what does that show to us? It presents an accommodation between the difficulties faced by both Kennedy in the US and Khrushchev in the Soviet Union. How the crisis is resolved is a kind of agreement between the two. Cuba runs out of missiles. Soviet ships return. And the Americans, on the other hand, declare a commitment never to invade Cuba again, which is important to the Soviets because it allows the Soviets to demonstrate that they are in a position to protect their allies from the Americans. And they also make the Americans commit to withdrawing the missiles they had in Turkey that are within range of Soviet territory.

Why is it important? It's a resolution that allows the two actors to communicate to their domestic audiences that they won the contest. Kennedy can go into the US and claim that he stopped the Soviets from advancing. Khrushchev can go into the Soviet Union and tell its bureaucracy that not only was he able to protect the Cubans, he was also able to extract concessions from the Americans that Stalin was unable to make. So, in a sense, the outcome of that game can be read more from the point of view of how those leaders sell that outcome to their domestic audiences, than from the point of view of how much it reflects the distribution of power in the international system.

Allison seeks to develop a reflection that proposes both a theoretical and analytical critique that realism is incapable of understanding the complexity of the decision process, and how this process actually takes place. By failing to understand this, realism endorses strategies that are making the international system increasingly vulnerable to the incidence of an event that we cannot control and that will have unpredictable consequences. We have a theoretical critique and a political critique. There is a problem with endorsing the narrative that realism proposes for making policy choices when this degree of risk is involved.

This marked a lot of the context of the context called strategic stability, in which we have the design of deterrence, which will generate a lot of strength after the Kennedy administration. That's all! Thanks for watching!
